question: Why is aciclovir selectively toxic to herpes-infected cells and largely harmless to uninfected human cells?

answers.text: Aciclovir is phosphorylated to its active triphosphate form exclusively by viral thymidine kinase (TK), which is present only in virus-infected cells.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Viral TK phosphorylates aciclovir ~3000 times more efficiently than human TK. Only in HSV/VZV-infected cells does the drug reach concentrations sufficient to inhibit viral DNA polymerase — an elegant example of selective toxicity.

answers.text: Aciclovir enters only virus-infected cells because its receptor is a viral surface protein.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aciclovir is a small nucleoside analogue taken up passively by all cells. Selectivity is conferred by differential phosphorylation inside the cell, not by receptor-mediated entry.

answers.text: Aciclovir inhibits human DNA polymerase, but viral DNA polymerase is 100× more sensitive to this inhibition.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While viral DNA polymerase IS more sensitive to aciclovir triphosphate than host polymerase, the primary selectivity mechanism is the viral TK-dependent activation step, not differential polymerase sensitivity alone.

answers.text: Aciclovir is degraded rapidly by human cell enzymes before it can exert any effect in uninfected cells.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aciclovir is not rapidly degraded in human cells. Its selectivity is based on the activation step (viral TK phosphorylation), not on differential degradation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Anti-Herpetic Drugs block. Aciclovir selectivity: activated only in herpes-infected cells by viral TK → active triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase.
Well done. Viral TK-dependent activation is the textbook example of pro-drug selective toxicity — it is also why TK-deficient viral mutants are aciclovir-resistant.
